text: Approach so far. Batch 1 mapped raw features: the panel is dominated by short horizon cross sectional mean reversion, peaking around 5 to 10 days, with reversal decaying to zero by 20 days and no usable long horizon momentum in Sharpe terms. Note that because the harness rank weights cross sectionally, any monotone cross sectional transform (cs_rank, cs_z, neg) is order preserving, so neg only flips the sign and I do not need to test both directions. Batches 2 to 4 established the winning template: standardize the raw predictor per name over time with ts_z, then scale cross sectionally by inverse realized volatility. Both steps help for different reasons. The ts_z step puts every name on a comparable surprise scale so the cross sectional ranking is not dominated by structurally high volatility names, and it raises rank IC. The inverse volatility step is a risk scaling that lowers portfolio volatility and raises Sharpe, though it lowers IC when pushed too far, which is the signature of risk reduction rather than better prediction. Two distinct predictor families emerged: reversal of the 5 day return and range position measured by minr, the price relative to its rolling n day low. minr carries the higher rank IC and is the more attractive base. Guardrails for final selection: prefer candidates with high SR AND high IC over pure Sharpe maximizers, avoid deep volatility division stacking such as dividing by std squared or cubed which buys Sharpe purely through low volatility tilt and is likely to be fragile out of sample, and keep the final three structurally simple and drawn from more than one predictor family.

text: Final selection rationale. The winning structure is an equal weight cross sectional blend of two legs, each built as standardize per name over time then scale by inverse realized volatility. Leg one is range position: neg(minr(60)), the negated price relative to its rolling 60 day low, ts_z standardized then divided by std. Leg two is return asymmetry: neg(skew(60)), negated 60 day return skew, standardized then divided by std. The two legs are close to uncorrelated in origin, one is a price level and path feature and the other a higher moment of the return distribution, and blending them lifted train SR from about 2.6 for the best single leg to about 2.9 to 3.0. Robustness evidence I relied on rather than raw peak SR. First, the whole blend family sits on a plateau of 2.93 to 3.06 across every denominator choice tested, std(20), std(40), std(60), std(120), sums of two std terms, and a product of two std terms, so the result does not hinge on one denominator cell. Second, the minr(60) core survived a deliberate stress test across ts_z windows 40, 60, 120 and 250 and across six denominators, scoring 2.10 to 2.63 throughout, so it is a ridge and not a single cell artifact, even though the minr lookback dimension itself is peaked at 60 versus 40 and 120. Third, delaying the core signal by three days cut SR from 2.59 to 1.31, confirming a genuine short horizon decaying effect rather than a static low volatility tilt that would survive any delay. Guarding against selection bias, I did not simply take the argmax of roughly forty near identical blends. I picked one top cell whose immediate neighbours all score above 2.95, one deliberately different parameterization using std(60) on both legs and the alternate skew z window to decorrelate the parameter choice, and one three leg variant that adds the short horizon reversal leg div(ts_z(neg(minr(10)), 120), std(60)). That third pick trades about nine percent of train SR for a twenty five percent higher rank IC of 0.0172, buying real predictive breadth as a hedge in case the minr(60) and skew(60) pair degrades out of sample.

top3_chosen: add(add(cs_z(div(ts_z(neg(minr(60)), 60), std(120))), cs_z(div(ts_z(neg(skew(60)), 120), std(40)))), cs_z(div(ts_z(neg(minr(10)), 120), std(60))))
rationale: All three are equal weight cross sectional blends built on one template: standardize a predictor per name over time with ts_z, then scale cross sectionally by inverse realized volatility. Leg one is range position, the negated price relative to its rolling 60 day low; leg two is negated 60 day return skew. The panel is dominated by short horizon cross sectional mean reversion, and range position captures it better than raw returns while skew adds a distribution shape effect that is largely independent. Both normalization steps are essential: raw neg(minr(60)) scores only 0.63 and vol scaling without ts_z scores 0.48 with negative IC, while the standardized and vol scaled version reaches 2.6 and the two leg blend reaches 2.9 to 3.1. I selected for plateau membership rather than peak SR. The blend family scores 2.93 to 3.06 across every denominator variant tested, and the minr(60) core holds 2.10 to 2.63 across four ts_z windows and six denominators, so neither pick depends on a single lucky cell. A three day delay cuts core SR from 2.59 to 1.31, confirming a genuine decaying short horizon effect rather than a static low volatility tilt. Pick one is a top cell whose neighbours all exceed 2.95; pick two uses a deliberately different parameterization, std(60) on both legs with the alternate skew z window, to decorrelate the parameter choice; pick three adds a short horizon reversal leg, giving up about nine percent of train SR for a twenty five percent higher rank IC of 0.0172 as breadth insurance.
